what inspection looks for — color, shape, symmetry, movement, and visible wounds or skin changes

claims.claim: Inspection is the physical exam technique of visually examining the body — the first of the four assessment techniques performed when assessing a body area.

In the focused assessment sequence, inspection is always performed first: for the thorax, the nurse first performs a visual inspection of the chest for symmetry and configuration, and only then palpation and auscultation.

The general survey — the observation of the patient's overall appearance, behavior, mobility, grooming, and skin color or tone — begins at the first meeting with the patient, so assessment by inspection starts at first sight.
Skin color and tone findings observed during inspection include pallor, jaundice, cyanosis, and flushing, each with a different clinical significance.

Inspection of a body area involves visually examining its external structures for abnormalities, asymmetry, swelling, and skin changes; the skin of the face, neck, and scalp is inspected for color, texture, and lesions.

Because inspection is performed before palpation and auscultation, visual findings are collected before the examiner touches the patient or listens with a stethoscope; looking disturbs nothing, so the exam captures the body's undisturbed state first.

Inspection is a low-cost, noninvasive, observation-based technique with no equipment requirement, which makes it safe to apply broadly across the whole patient — the basis of the lesson's framing that inspection is the cheapest diagnostic tool.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the general survey and inspection are two different things or one technique at two scales.
positions: OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills 15.1 presents the general survey as observation of the whole patient — appearance, behavior, mobility, grooming, and skin color or tone.
OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills 23.2 and 22.1 present inspection as the first technique of the physical exam, applied to specific body areas (chest, head and neck).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the general survey as inspection at its widest scale — applied to the whole patient starting at first meeting — and focused inspection as the same skill applied to one body area during the exam. This is faithful to both sections and keeps the lesson unified around one technique.

conflictingEvidence.issue: The phrase 'inspection is the cheapest diagnostic tool' is a framing idea, not a quotation from any source.
positions: The sources describe inspection as visual observation that requires no equipment and is performed before other techniques.
No source uses the 'cheapest diagnostic tool' wording.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the phrase as its own framing, grounded in the sources' description of inspection as free, fast, noninvasive visual observation; it is presented as the lesson's framing rather than attributed to any source.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated placeholder for this topic (generic 'foundational concept in Nursing & Allied Health Foundations' boilerplate with no clinical content, if present in the generated draft store) carried no verifiable clinical substance and was discarded; all content was researched from OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills.

correctionsNeeded: Attributed the working definition of inspection to OpenStax Clinical Nursing Skills (visual examination of external structures) rather than leaving it unattributed.
Established the exam order explicitly from the thorax section: inspection first, then palpation, then auscultation.
Named the inspection targets (color, shape, symmetry, movement, wounds/skin changes) and the general survey categories (appearance, behavior, mobility, grooming, skin color/tone) from the sources.

All examples are original (Mr. Delgado at the doorway, Ms. Nguyen's knee visit, the stomach-pain admission); none are taken from any source.
